questions.q: Identify the exposition of "इग्योकु की <ksyd" — what initial situation, characters, and setting are established in the opening paragraphs?
questions.a: The exposition establishes a remote village (vekoL;k) on a festival day (tkM+s dk fnu), introducing Yagyu (yq^u) as a young, gifted flautist whose music is woven into the village's daily rhythms — children playing, women working, the natural soundscape. A wrong answer (e.g., starting with Yagyu at the court) reveals the student cannot distinguish the story's chronological beginning from its dramatic high point, confusing exposition with rising action.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the narrative structure uses the arrival of the new king (नया राजा) as a structural turning point. What changes in the narrative pace and focus after this event?
questions.a: The new king's arrival marks the climax: the narrative pace accelerates — short, dramatic sentences replace the earlier lyrical descriptions; focus shifts from Yagyu's music to political upheaval (court intrigue, name change of the village, imposition of new order). After this, the narrative slows into falling action as Yagyu returns to the village. A wrong answer that treats the new king as just another character shows the student misses how structural devices (pace, focus, tone) signal thematic shifts.

questions.q: Apply the concept of 'rising action' to trace three specific events that escalate Yagyu's journey from village flautist to court musician. Quote or paraphrase textual evidence for each.
questions.a: 1) Yagyu's music captivates the old king during a hunt (जंगल में शिकार के दौरान राजा का ध्यान आकर्षित करना). 2) The king grants him patronage, giving him land and a house (राजा द्वारा जमीन और घर देना). 3) Yagyu becomes the official court musician, his flute now signaling royal routines (दरबारी संगीतकार के रूप में नियुक्ति, बांसुरी से राजकीय कार्यक्रमों का संचालन). A wrong answer listing only one event or vague descriptions shows inability to identify causal links in rising action.

questions.q: Analyze how the narrative structure uses contrast between the 'old village' (opening) and the 'changed village' (ending) to deepen the story's meaning. Identify two specific contrasts in imagery or routine.
questions.a: Contrast 1: Opening — village wakes to flute's tune organically (children, women, nature respond); Ending — village wakes to factory sirens, forced routines, silence where music was. Contrast 2: Opening — king and villagers share intimate bond (king knows every flautist by name); Ending — new king imposes alien administration, villagers become subjects. A wrong answer that only notes 'things changed' without textual contrasts shows superficial reading, missing structural parallelism.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the resolution (Yagyu playing for his grandchildren in the transformed village) provides closure or irony. Justify with two reasons from the narrative structure.
questions.a: It is ironic closure: structurally, the story returns to the opening image (flautist playing in village), but the context is inverted — the audience is now his own grandchildren, not the whole village; the music is a private act, not communal lifeblood. The narrative circle closes, but the center has shifted from collective culture to individual memory. A wrong answer calling it 'happy ending' ignores structural irony and the author's critical stance on cultural erasure.

questions.q: Create a brief narrative outline (5 bullet points) for a modern retelling of this story set in a contemporary Indian town, preserving the same five-stage plot structure but changing the art form and patronage system.
questions.a: A strong answer maps each stage: 1) Exposition — a street rapper in a basti whose verses reflect local life. 2) Rising action — a media corporation 'discovers' him, offers contract. 3) Climax — corporate rebranding strips his lyrics of local dialect, imposes commercial formula. 4) Falling action — he returns to basti, now gentrified, his old audience displaced. 5) Resolution — he raps for his niece on a balcony, the beat echoing but the community gone. A weak answer that just lists modern elements without structural parallelism shows inability to transfer narrative architecture.
